sections.h2: Which office covers your Ossining house?
sections.html:
Ossining is a Hudson River town containing two incorporated villages, the Village of Ossining and part of Briarcliff Manor, and an unincorporated area outside both. The town's Building Department answers only for that unincorporated area. If your lot sits within a village, permits and occupancy questions belong to the village, so confirm your location first.

The town covers 15.74 square miles, with the Hudson on its west edge and the Croton River on the north. Ossining Union Free School District serves the town. Put the district on every document, since the state seller form asks for it.

Ossining town had 39,964 residents in 13,711 households as of July 2025. About 62.8 percent of homes are owner-occupied, with a typical value of $552,900, while the median rent is $2,203. Households with a mortgage carry a median monthly cost of $3,774, and the median household income is $125,539. Low turnover (89.5 percent stayed put over the past year) means a tidy house with complete records tends to draw notice.

The 2025 assessment roll followed a town reappraisal, so a buyer who compares your figure with a neighbor's is looking at fairly fresh numbers. Tyler Technologies helped with the project, and data collectors visited properties in yellow vests with ID badges. The town updates its assessment records every year.

Stop by the Assessor's Office at 16 Croton Avenue, 3rd Floor, or phone, before you list. Look over your property record for mistakes like a wrong bedroom count or an addition that was never recorded. Staff will talk through an assessment with you at any time. Weekday hours are 8:30 am to 4:30 pm. From July 1 through September 1, expect every town office but the Town Clerk to close at 3:15 pm on Fridays.

Watch for scam callers posing as the Building Department and asking for more application money. Any message that pushes you to pay should be checked by calling the department at the number on the town website.

The Board of Assessment Review hears complaints, and its meeting falls on the third Tuesday in June, the date the state gives for Westchester town boards. Sessions are held late afternoon into evening, so working owners can attend.

Submit the state complaint form with a grievance questionnaire and evidence of market value: what you paid recently, comparable sales or an appraisal. Pleas based on what you can afford, or on how little you use public services, do not count. You will hear back by September 15. If the result disappoints you and you live in your one, two or three family home, a Small Claims Assessment Review is the next step, and you can handle it without a lawyer.

Filing a deed with the Westchester County Clerk starts at a $45 statutory fee. Add $5 for every written side of a page, $5 for the residential TP-584 and $125 for the RP-5217 transfer report. The clerk's own sample, a three-page residential deed in a single municipality, totals $190.

State transfer tax is two dollars on each $500 of the sale price, and a leftover partial $500 is rounded up. It falls on the seller by default. Buyers of a $1 million or higher residence pay an added 1 percent mansion tax.

  • The county's Property Records Electronic Portal calculates the fees for each submission.
  • Transfer tax can be paid by ACH, certified check, bank check, attorney escrow check or approved vendor check.
  • Credit cards cover ordinary fees up to $500 but never taxes.

Your title company or attorney will probably do the filing. Ask who is submitting the deed and on what day.

sections.h2: What must an Ossining seller reveal about flooding and condition?
sections.html:
Under Real Property Law 462, a seller of a house with up to four units must fill in the state's form and hand it over ahead of the buyer's signature on the contract. Two rivers bound this town, so read the flood questions closely.

The form asks about FEMA floodplain status, flood insurance, any flood claim you filed, and whether water ever entered the building through heavy rain, storm surge, tidal inundation or river overflow. It also covers shared or leased areas, septic or public sewer, a sump pump, the roof and any radon testing. An owner who later learns something that makes an earlier answer wrong owes the buyer a corrected form. An as-is sale is still legal, but the form must be delivered either way.

Do you have a deck, shed or finished basement built without a permit? Ask the Building Department, or your village, whether the permit can still be closed. Certificates of occupancy come up on the form too.

Most sales follow the same order. First, learn whether your lot is in the town or a village. Check your assessment record for errors. Answer the state seller form, closing out any open permit questions with the right office. Choose an attorney or title company, who will prepare the deed, Form TP-584 and the RP-5217 transfer report. At closing the transfer tax is paid, the deed is filed with the Westchester County Clerk, and any loan payoff comes out of your proceeds.

Skipping an early step usually costs time later, because the title company cannot record a deed with missing forms.

Cash works best for a house with problems that a retail buyer's inspector would flag. With no lender underwriting, timing rests on title, payoff letters and the recording steps described above. After an owner's death, an attorney can say which estate papers the title company needs prior to signing a deed.

Get offers in writing, find out who covers transfer tax and recording, and confirm the buyer can truly close when promised. For questions about your own assessment or exemptions, the Assessor's Office is the right place, not a buyer.

Before talking price, line up your deed, current tax bill, permits for earlier projects, and payoff letters on any loan or lien. A buyer can then start title work immediately, which protects the closing date. Also decide ahead of time which rooms and systems you will disclose as needing repair, so the seller form and the contract say the same thing.

faqs.q: Does the Town Building Department cover a house in the Village of Ossining?
faqs.a: No. The department has jurisdiction only in the unincorporated area outside the village limits. For a house in the Village of Ossining or the Briarcliff Manor part of the town, ask that village about permits and certificates.

faqs.q: What is the deadline for an Ossining assessment complaint?
faqs.a: Grievance Day, the third Tuesday in June. The tentative roll comes out June 1, and the Board of Assessment Review is the first stop before any other remedy.

faqs.q: Who pays transfer tax on an Ossining sale?
faqs.a: Usually the seller, at two dollars per $500 of price with partial amounts rounded up, unless the contract shifts it. The buyer owes the extra 1 percent mansion tax only on residences of $1 million or more.

faqs.q: Do I owe a buyer the state's seller disclosure form in Ossining?
faqs.a: Yes, for a house of up to four units. Get the signed form to the buyer or the buyer's agent before the contract is signed. Condo and co-op apartments are outside the rule.

faqs.q: Who records the deed for an Ossining house?
faqs.a: The Westchester County Clerk's Land Records Division. A deed costs $45 plus $5 per page, and cover pages and transfer forms are prepared in the county's online portal. For fee questions call (914) 995-3094.
